inline.s: From the summary given above, we can see that the phrase in the general heading covers two distinct matters. “Said” refers to the speaking; “Dharma” refers to the Dharma-door.

“Therefore” is a word that gathers up what precedes and opens what follows. “Apart from all marks” — this is what the Elder meant above when he spoke of being apart from all marks. Whatever marks of self, person, being, and life, and whatever confronting marks of Dharma and non-Dharma, and so on — none of them is not to be left behind; hence “all.” “Should” is a word of decision, making clear that nothing short of total detachment will do. Earlier the Elder said that one who is apart from all marks is named a Buddha, showing that only by being apart from marks does one attain the great accomplishment — that was spoken with respect to the fruition. That is where the Elder’s deep understanding tended. After the World-Honored One confirmed his approval, He went on to speak of the first pāramitā and of patience, the two sections that show one should be apart from all marks in cultivating the six pāramitās — that was spoken with respect to the causal cultivation. This section takes up that meaning and gathers it back into the resolve for bodhi made while apart from all marks, which is a further step still. For cultivating the six pāramitās is the cause of accomplishment, while the resolve for bodhi is again the cause that initiates the cultivation. Here we have come right down to the source. Whether fruition, cultivation, or the causal mind, being apart from marks runs through them all from first to last. So the Elder deeply understood where it all converges, and the World-Honored One further clarified from where it arises, so that we may know: only when apart from all marks is one named a Buddha; therefore one should be apart from marks in advancing the cultivation, and apart from marks in making the resolve. Then prajñā is the Dharma-door that runs through beginning and end, and being apart from marks is the road that turns the ordinary into the noble — this should now be clearly understood.

The way this section gathers up the meaning of what precedes is not limited to what was said above — it does not merely gather the several sections that come before. You should know that the two phrases “should be apart from all marks” and “resolve for bodhi” are the very dot that brings to life all those earlier statements at the opening of the sutra: “one who has resolved for bodhi should thus abide, should thus subdue his mind.” Why? Because resolving for bodhi while apart from all marks is precisely why the mind that abides in marks must be subdued. Nor is that all: it also gathers into one the whole meaning of “all classes of living beings,” and so on, from the answer given at the opening of the sutra. Why? Because to save boundless living beings and cause them to enter nirvāṇa without residue is to resolve for anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi; and “in truth there is no living being who attains extinction” is being apart from all marks. The sense is as if to say: what was answered before — causing beings to be saved while having no mark of saving — is because one must be apart from all marks, and only then is what one has resolved truly the bodhi mind. Why? Because one who cannot be apart from marks can never save all living beings to the end, nor cause them to enter nirvāṇa without residue; then what is resolved becomes an empty vow. That is why it was also said just before: “if there are marks of self, person, and so on, then one is not a bodhisattva.” So here it does not say “in resolving for bodhi one should be apart from all marks,” but “one should be apart from all marks in resolving for bodhi” — the meaning is very pointed. Did it not say earlier? Bodhi is enlightenment, is equality, is compassion. If one clings to marks, then one’s mind is not enlightenment, not equality, not unconditioned kindness, not compassion of one substance. Though one may call it a resolve, can what is resolved be called the bodhi mind? Therefore one should assuredly be apart from all marks, and only then is it a resolve for bodhi.

The three phrases that follow — “should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas,” and “should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing” — explain this section’s meaning of being apart from all marks. Spoken with reference to those, what is said here is likewise a summarizing expression. Hence the section heading says “summarizing and concluding”: “summarizing” shows that it gives rise to what follows; “concluding” shows that it gathers up what precedes.
(Mao) Second: Explaining and establishing.
“He should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form; he should not give rise to a mind dwelling on sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; he should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing.”

This section explains and establishes the “should be apart from all marks” of the preceding passage. Yet it does not offer a separate explanation; it simply quotes the passage on giving rise to the non-abiding mind from the earlier part concerning the causal aspect, varying its wording slightly — this is how the Buddha taught Dharma, so exquisitely wrought, so perfectly complete from every side. Spoken thus, it not only clarifies the meaning of the preceding section but also illuminates the section on giving rise to the non-abiding mind, lest those who hear the earlier teaching fail to fuse the principle. It thereby echoes the preceding text and brings it to a close. How supremely skillful!

“Give rise” means to bring forth. One who resolves for bodhi should neither let the mind scatter nor let it sink. If it sinks, from where could the six pāramitās and all practices be undertaken? Hence the word “give rise” is used with special emphasis to convey this. The sense of this section is as if to say: a moment ago it was said that one should be apart from all marks in resolving for bodhi — apart from what marks? And how should one be apart? There is nothing else: since one is bringing forth the enlightened mind of equality and compassion, then when that mind rises, one should free it from the confronting dust-realms of form, sound, and the rest, and not dwell or cling. Then all marks are left behind. One should only give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing at all amid all confronting dust-realms; then what is resolved is indeed anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The earlier text says, “he should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing” — that is spoken in division, to make clear the meaning of clinging to neither the empty nor the existent extreme. The present text says, “he should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing” — that is spoken in union. The wording is slightly expanded, but the meaning is finer and more penetrating, entirely unlike the earlier passage. For it fears that those who heard the earlier teaching might split non-abiding and giving rise to mind into two separate pieces, so that they would either cling to non-abiding and fall into emptiness, or cling to giving rise to mind and stagnate in existence. Even if not, simply failing to fuse non-abiding and giving rise to mind means the two extremes of empty and existent cannot both be dissolved. Though one may cling to neither extreme and accord with the Middle Way, the marks of middle and extreme still stand plain before one. Thus, though not clinging to the extremes, one still clings to the middle. Where there is clinging, there is discrimination, and one still falls into the four marks. So now the Buddha melts them into one whole, saying: what was earlier called giving rise to a mind that dwells on nothing was never two things; it is simply that one should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing. This makes clear that when the mind rises is precisely when it does not abide, and when it does not abide is precisely when the mind rises. Then the existent is the empty and the empty is the existent; empty and existent are simultaneously and together present. If one can hold empty and existent as simultaneous, then there is no such thing as empty or existent, no such thing as extreme, and no such thing as middle. Every place and every moment is nothing but the middle — this is what is called perfect middle. Reaching perfect middle, self and Dharma are both emptied, the four propositions all dismissed; this is the utmost of marklessness, and only this is resolving for the supreme bodhi of being apart from all marks. How could a beginner at resolve be capable of this? Precisely because he cannot, it says “should” — meaning one should thus know, one should thus learn.

The earlier section on giving rise to the non-abiding mind, spoken with respect to the causal aspect, was itself the gathering-point of all the meanings spoken after the sutra opened. Now this section, since it gathers up the earlier meaning of non-abiding resolve and is followed by the next section gathering up the earlier meaning of non-abiding giving, is clearly the grand gathering-point of all meanings since the sutra opened. Hence the heading reads “concluding the preceding text.”

In the earlier passage on giving rise to the non-abiding mind, “all bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas” refers to those who resolve for bodhi. “Pure” means being apart from all marks. You should know that the pure mind is the original nature — what is called one’s original face. It is what the ten dharma-realms all share in common, and so it is also named the one true dharma-realm. But the pure mind of the six ordinary classes of living beings has long been obstructed by the confronting marks of self and person and the like, and so cannot appear. To the extent that marks are left behind, to that extent the pure mind appears. The earlier saying, “when the mind of faith is pure, then true marks arise,” refers to this. True marks is another name for the original nature. As one leaves marks behind stage by stage, this is called partial realization of enlightenment. At the very first stage of leaving one portion behind, this is the first stage of partial realization, named the bodhisattva of the initial dwelling. This is the first step in turning the ordinary into the noble, also called the group of right concentration. “Right concentration” means abiding; “group” means class. It means that one has entered the class of noble fruition and will never retreat from anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi; hence “group of right concentration.” Only at this stage can one be said to have accomplished the root of faith. Because the root of faith is accomplished, one attains non-retreat. Because one first accomplishes the noble fruition of non-retreat, it is named the initial dwelling. Passing through all forty-one stages and cutting off the last portion of ignorance, only then are all marks left completely behind, and the pure mind appears in full — this is called ultimate enlightenment, also named wonderful enlightenment, and also called Buddha. From this we can see that from ordinary being to ultimate enlightenment, the whole endeavor is nothing but being apart from marks. How can one be apart from them? By relying on the prajñā of words and bringing forth the prajñā of contemplation. The World-Honored One feared that students might not deeply understand the prajñā of words spoken above, and then from what would they contemplate? So He spoke to this point and further fused the earlier meanings, to make contemplation and practice workable. Gentlemen, you should know that since we have taken up and upheld this sutra, we must thoroughly comprehend the purport of what the Buddha taught, making it clear and luminous in the mind. Only then, when cultivating any Dharma and meeting any circumstance, can we apply it to pass through affairs and train the mind.

All the more should you, while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, while dressing and eating, while greeting guests and seeing them off — at all times and in all places — constantly keep the meaning you have comprehended in your mind, dwelling in it and steeping in it, never letting it be interrupted. Strive to melt the sutra’s meaning and this mind into one piece. This itself is habituation; this itself is contemplation. You need not necessarily sit in meditation to contemplate. Practicing thus, you can cause ignorance gradually to thin and lessen, and you will gain the power to increase bodhi and the capacity to dismiss clinging and break the self. Moreover, only by nurturing this steadily can you apply it when the time comes — this is what was earlier called nourishing the mind of the Way. Cultivated thus, the eye of the Way will become ever clearer. This is the most intimate and savory method of practice, costing no effort and no trouble, yet yielding great benefit — never neglect it.

If the earlier text and the present text are joined and read together, the meaning becomes clearer. Let me now link the preceding and following texts into one continuous whole and expound it for you, so that you may comprehend it thoroughly. It runs: one who resolves for anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi should cause the intrinsically possessed pure mind of self-nature to appear. How is it to appear? This mind should not give rise to the six dust-realms; it should not dwell in dust-realms and manifest its mind, and thereby gradually attain purity. From this we can know that “purity” does not mean sinking into emptiness and stagnating in stillness, making the mind not rise. It means only being apart from all marks. Apart from what marks? It means one should not dwell or give rise to mind upon the marks of the six dusts, which are discriminating and confronting. And not only should one be apart from the marks of objects, one should also be apart from the mark of splitting non-abiding and giving rise to mind into two things, and so give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing. What does it mean to give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing? The Chan Master Yongjia Yuanjue of the Tang has a verse that serves perfectly as a commentary on this. The verse runs: “Just when one applies the mind, / just then there is no mind applied; / with no mind just applying, / constantly applying, constantly none.” The first line is giving rise to mind, is the existent, is illumination. The second line is dwelling on nothing, is the empty, is negation. Seen together, they are giving rise to a mind that dwells on nothing, which is precisely empty and existent as mutually identical, negation and illumination simultaneous. The third line is giving rise to mind precisely while non-abiding — what is called negating while illuminating, being existent while empty. The fourth line is non-abiding precisely while giving rise to mind — what is called illuminating while negating, being empty while existent. Read the third and fourth lines together, and negation, illumination, empty, existent, non-abiding, and giving rise to mind are all beyond speech, and yet are precisely giving rise to a mind that dwells on nothing. This is the meaning of being at ease in both dissolving and sustaining. You should know that giving rise to the non-abiding mind is giving rise to the pure mind; giving rise to the pure mind is giving rise to true marks. Upholding the Diamond Prajñā, one should thus believe, understand, and uphold it; one should thus speak it for others, so that self and others alike are thus and thus apart from all marks, and thus and thus manifest the pure mind they share in common. Only this is resolving for anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The earlier section on giving rise to the non-abiding mind was spoken after the adornment of Buddha-lands. The present section, gathering up the non-abiding resolve, comes after the six pāramitās. This again highlights that cultivating the six pāramitās is precisely the adornment of Buddha-lands. Thus the present passage, expounding that one should be apart from all marks in resolving and cultivating the six pāramitās, precisely gathers up and reveals the earlier meaning that one should be apart from marks in adorning Buddha-lands. The reason a bodhisattva adorns Buddha-lands is that his intent is to seek above and transform below. Therefore in both seeking above and transforming below he should be apart from all marks. It is said in the Buddhist scriptures: “Above, there is no Buddha-way to accomplish; below, there are no living beings to save.” This means accomplishing Buddhahood without seeing a mark of accomplishment, and saving living beings without seeing a mark of saving.

In sum, giving rise to a mind that dwells on nothing is the true exposition of being apart from all marks. This is what is called perfect detachment. Perfect detachment means emptying through to the very bottom — it is dismissing the four propositions, cutting off the hundred negations; it is the non-obstruction of principle, the non-obstruction of phenomena, the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena, and the non-obstruction of phenomenon with phenomenon. It is negating and illuminating together, dissolving and sustaining together, negation and illumination simultaneous, dissolving and sustaining at ease. You should comprehend it thus. Again, folding non-abiding into the giving rise to mind is extremely pointed. It instructs the student that if he gives rise to mind apart from non-abiding, then his mind has abiding; and when it rises, it becomes wrong. How subtle, how perilous! The next section reverses this and makes the meaning plain.
(Mao) Third: Reversing to reveal.
“If the mind has abiding, then it is non-abiding.”

“If the mind has abiding” — this makes plain that if one gives rise to mind apart from non-abiding, then the mind that rises has abiding. “Abiding” means grasping and clinging. If one gives rise to mind apart from non-abiding, then one’s mind has grasping. Grasping means clinging to marks. Hence “then it is non-abiding” — meaning that to abide is to be wrong. Why? Because abiding means there are marks, which contradicts the earlier statement that one should be apart from all marks; hence it is wrong. Reading these two lines of sutra text in one breath, the meaning is very clear. “If the mind has abiding, then it is non-abiding” is like saying: if the mind has something to abide in, that is not what it should abide in. Hence “to abide is to be wrong.” This meaning stands in exact contrast with the opening of the sutra, where it is said that the bodhisattva should abide as taught — one positive, one negative, echoing each other from afar. If the mind has abiding, then it is not abiding as taught; hence “then it is non-abiding.” The earlier statement that one should abide as taught closely follows the preceding words that one should dwell on nothing. From this we can see that “abide as taught” is said only because the questioner asked how one should abide, and so the Buddha provisionally followed along and spoke of abiding. Its real meaning is abiding that is non-abiding. In other words, one should abide in non-abiding. This is enough to prove that one should abide in nothing at all. If the mind has abiding, then abiding is wrong.

Someone may say: your meaning is not right. The sutra text means that if the mind has abiding in any dharma, then it is not abiding in prajñā. It makes clear that one should not abide in any dharma, but should abide in prajñā only. Does the Great Prajñā Sutra not say: “Not abiding in any dharma is itself abiding in prajñā”? If the two passages are checked against each other, it is clear that this passage means one should abide in prajñā. If one abides in prajñā, one cannot but not abide in any dharma. Hence “if the mind has abiding, then it is non-abiding.” So your meaning is not right. Such a person’s words are greatly mistaken, greatly mistaken, because he has not understood the sutra’s meaning. Now, fearing that some may see what the Great Prajñā Sutra says and misunderstand, I cannot but cite it and explain the meaning thoroughly. You should know that this sutra above specially spoke of the first pāramitā and of patience, precisely to make clear that prajñā is not apart from all dharmas and all dharmas are not apart from prajñā. This alone proves that the phrase “then it is non-abiding” can by no means be taken as “not abiding in prajñā.” Why? Since prajñā and all dharmas cannot be apart from each other, the Great Prajñā Sutra’s “not abiding in any dharma” already includes “not abiding in prajñā” within it. And as for its further words “is itself abiding in prajñā,” one should grasp them at the words “is itself.” For it means that not abiding in anything is itself abiding. In sum, it makes clear the meaning that prajñā should take non-abiding as its abiding. This is exactly the same in sense as this sutra’s “he should only abide as taught.” Moreover, besides these two lines, the Great Prajñā Sutra has two more: “Not believing in any dharma is named believing in prajñā.” You should know that all dharmas are spoken by the Buddha — how could one not believe them? If the four lines are read together, one can awaken to the fact that they too make clear the meaning that all dharmas cannot be apart from prajñā, and that every practitioner cannot be apart from prajñā. But if one takes them to mean that all dharmas are unnecessary and one need only cling to a single prajñā, then the Buddha-Dharma would be swept from the earth. Is such a principle conceivable? As for this sutra’s saying plainly above that prajñā is not prajñā, and again that the first is not first — how could it be said that one should abide in prajñā? In sum, whoever reads Buddhist sutras and wishes to understand Buddhist principle must understand deeply and comprehensively. Otherwise he may mistake the Dharma and mistake people. The prajñā Dharma-door especially demands care, for its principle is profoundly subtle and its words are exceedingly flexible. It can never be peered at with shallow views or measured with biased ones.

There are also those who suspect that the words “non-abiding” mean “then one is not abiding in bodhi” — this too is a great error. The Buddha and the Elder, to make clear that the bodhi mind also should not be abided in, deliberately spoke the latter half of the sutra; when we reach that latter half its purport will be clear, and I will not elaborate here. In sum, abiding is grasping, and also clinging. Since one should neither grasp nor cling to anything, one should not abide in anything, and where there is abiding there is wrongness.

Someone may again say: the sutra says one should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas; then “apart from marks” seems to be spoken only with respect to the existent extreme. He does not realize that in speaking the one word “dharmas,” non-dharmas are already included. Did it not say earlier: “the Dharma itself should be let go of, how much more non-Dharma”? So when dharmas are spoken of, non-dharmas are included. Moreover it says plainly that one should be apart from all marks. If the four propositions of existent and non-existent were not all included, it could not be called “all.” In all such places, if one does not contemplate deeply and comprehensively, one is giving a shallow account of prajñā. Whether one speaks wildly or shallowly, the offense is very great. So now, taking this occasion, I will analyze and explain it in detail.

These two sections — gathering up the non-abiding resolve and the non-abiding giving — since they conclude the preceding text, contain many meanings, and important ones. If they are not brought out thoroughly layer by layer, the purport will not be coherent, and how could one contemplate? Moreover, dwelling in dust and giving rise to mind is precisely the accumulated habit of ordinary beings, exceedingly hard to remove; while not dwelling in dust and giving rise to mind is precisely the medicine matched to the illness, of the utmost importance. So how can one manage not to abide? One simply cannot but speak of many expedients, so that there is a place to put one’s hand. Otherwise, though the principle of prajñā be stated most correctly, it is empty talk; though one hears it most clearly, one has heard nothing. Therefore in such places both speaker and listener should give it their extreme attention. One should not fear trouble; it admits of no slighting.

The Elder asked: one who resolves for anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi — how should he abide, how should he subdue his mind? These were asked separately, each on its own. For resolving, abiding, and subduing are plainly three matters. Yet though the words are three, the intent is one. Why? The Elder asked about abiding because his mind was set on finding a way for the mind to rest securely. Fearing it could not rest securely, he further asked how to subdue. And asking how to abide and subdue is precisely asking how one should resolve for bodhi. So the World-Honored One’s answer was likewise a fused answer. Look at the sense of the first answer on subduing, and you can awaken to the fact that what is called subduing is nothing else than subduing the marks in which one abides. Hence: “if there are the four marks, then one is not a bodhisattva.” That this saying is placed especially at the point of conclusion is precisely to bring this meaning to life. Next, when answering how to abide, He says only: “he should abide as taught.” And what was taught is precisely that one should dwell on nothing. Looking deeply into the sense, one can further awaken to the fact that because living beings abide and cling everywhere, they are told to be non-abiding; and telling them to be non-abiding is precisely how they are subdued. Thus abiding and subduing have already been fused into one. What follows is nothing but unfolding the meaning of “should dwell on nothing.” When He has spoken to this point, He again cites what was said before, varies its wording slightly, and speaks it more deeply and penetratingly: “he should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing.” And He says: “if the mind has abiding, then it is non-abiding.” From this one can further awaken to the fact that the two words “non-abiding” are the central purport of the Diamond Prajñā. The whole sutra’s thousand words and ten thousand phrases can be covered in a single phrase: non-abiding, and nothing more. Why did the World-Honored One fuse His answer thus? Why should the reader of the sutra thus grasp the central purport within that answer? Because otherwise one’s practice cannot seize the essential point; and failing to seize the essential point, how is one to set to work?

Furthermore, the “apart from all marks” spoken here is the meaning of non-abiding. The “should be apart” spoken here is the meaning of subduing. And to say “one should be apart from all marks in resolving for bodhi” is again to fuse abiding, subduing, and resolving into one. The sense is as if to say: the meanings spoken above must not be taken merely to mean that after resolving for bodhi one should subdue the marks in which one abides. You should know that at the very time of resolving, one should be apart from all marks and dwell on nothing — only then is it a resolve for bodhi. Gaining this conclusion, all that was said above becomes more pointed. One who hears the Dharma and understands this meaning knows that at the time of resolving there is no room for vagueness. Since the mind is true, one will not bring about crooked fruits. What is called “at the first arising of the resolve, one then accomplishes perfect enlightenment” is exactly thus, exactly thus. One should thus believe, understand, and uphold it.

“He should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form; he should not give rise to a mind dwelling on sound, fragrance, taste, touch, or dharmas.” The World-Honored One repeated these two lines because they truly carry deep meaning. For the environment of living beings in this dusty world never departs from these six. Dwelling in dust and giving rise to mind is an accumulated habit from beginningless time. And one who wishes to end birth and death must turn the back on dust and unite with enlightenment. So He deliberately repeated them again and again, so that living beings amid dust-realms should take the three words “should not dwell” deeply to heart, constantly contemplate them, and diligently keep far from them. Thus they may gradually come to be able not to abide.

Let us set aside form, sound, fragrance, and taste for the moment. Let us first speak of “dharmas”: how is one to be apart from them? Quite apart from the fact that worldly dharmas each carry duties one should fulfill, and if one fails in those duties one falls into causality again, how can one be apart? Moreover the Buddha-Dharma is also a dharma, and one must cultivate according to it — how much less can one be apart from that? So we know that what is called being apart, called non-abiding, means not clinging, not that one does not practice the dharma. Yet since one must do one’s utmost to practice it, how is one to practice so as to begin not clinging? Therefore expedients are indispensable. Let me now speak of expedients in both practice and understanding.

What are the expedients of practice? Speaking in terms of worldly dharmas: whatever one ought to do, one should of course do with all one’s heart and strength, without mistaking causality. But the first thing to guard is this — however hard and bitter the hardship, one must never give rise to a mind of toil and resentment; however excellent one’s achievement, one must never harbor the thought of claiming credit; and if unfortunately one fails, one must never on that account become afflicted and sorrowful, sighing and resentful. Only when this level is attained can one reach what was said before: when things come, respond; when things pass, forget — and thereby accord with non-clinging. Speaking in terms of world-transcending dharmas: the essential point is that however long, however well, however perfectly one has cultivated, one never considers oneself right and never becomes complacent. Thus one can reach the state of acting without affair.

Yet the reason living beings cling everywhere is that there is the mark of self, and the mark of self is born from the view of self. Therefore if one would solve the matter at the root, one must break the view of self. And to break the view of self, one must understand Buddhist principle. Why? The view of self arises from delusion. And as for the principle of no-self and the method of breaking the self, only the Buddhist scriptures expound them most finely and most fully. So without the Buddha-Dharma one cannot open one’s right wisdom, dissolve one’s obscurations, transform delusion, and remove the view of self. Therefore, if one would truly be able not to cling in one’s conduct, one must understand Buddhist principle. Yet understanding is by no means easy. Take the view of self as an example. How is there a view of self? What is the harm of the view of self? How can the view of self be removed? What exactly is no-self? Already the threads seem tangled enough. How much more so the many, many related principles and facts. If one knows one point and misses the rest, one will surely take a part for the whole. Partial clinging is itself clinging. So to understand a single principle or fact in the Buddhist scriptures, one must first do away with such partial clinging. Know that only by fusing all meanings can one penetrate a single meaning. This is why one should look from every side. Only by looking from every side can one gradually enter deep and comprehensive contemplation, and attain deep and comprehensive understanding.

What then are the expedients of understanding? First, one should read much and recite much; best of all, read through all the sutras and treatises. Yet to glance over them casually is of no benefit at all, and not everyone is able to do it. Let me here name only a very few of those that are indispensable: one should read much from such sutras as the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra, the Śūraṅgama, the Laṅkāvatāra, and the Kṣitigarbha. As for the Avataṃsaka and the Lotus, if one cannot read them through, one may read a single kind; if one cannot read them all, reading several chapters will do. The Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Vows from the Avataṃsaka should especially be upheld as a daily recitation. And that this sutra itself should not be parted from for a single day goes without saying. As for treatises, the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna and the Mahāyāna Śamatha-vipaśyanā should both be placed in one’s daily recitation and read in turn until familiar. And the three Pure Land sutras and the one treatise cannot be left unread either. Whenever one reads, one should read with utmost sincerity and reverence, reading with leisurely steeping. The essential lines within should be constantly kept and nourished in the mind, so that they fuse with one’s own mind into one. This is the most wonderful gate of contemplation.

Never may one regard them as ordinary books, merely dissecting and disputing within the words. The more one dissects, the heavier one’s clinging and the deeper one’s obstruction. Why? Because such a one is doing nothing but using the view of self and the ordinary emotions of many lives past to conjecture and surmise. Thus one not only increases partial clinging but may well give rise to great wrong views. Moreover, the principle spoken by Buddhas and bodhisattvas is itself beyond the reach of ordinary emotion. To measure it now with ordinary emotion — how can it be understood? Because it is not understood, one may even give rise to great slander and fall into the uninterrupted hell. It is not merely a matter of losing faith. Therefore prying into the scriptures by way of words is a great taboo in studying Buddhism. Hence the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra says: “To fathom the ocean of perfect enlightenment with the views of rebirth — there is no such possibility.”

As for the annotations and commentaries of the ancient virtuous ones, if one wishes to study them, one should read widely. Since each has its strong and weak points, one must reconcile their meanings, and must above all avoid partial clinging. Here too, as with reading sutras, one must not dissect and seek only within the words. Only as said above — reading with utmost sincerity and reverence, reading with leisurely steeping, keeping and nourishing, contemplating — is what matters most. In particular one must assist it by practice. First one should uphold the precepts and cultivate merit, add diligent repentance, revere the Three Jewels, and pray for their blessing, to dissolve one’s former obstructions and open one’s right view. And one should make great compassionate vows to save living beings widely. Then responses will come swiftly. Further, one should earnestly recite the Buddha’s name and mantras, relying on the power of blessing to remove one’s obscurations. Thus understanding and practice advance together, and after long effort without slackening, obstructions gradually lighten, the mind gradually empties, wisdom gradually opens; the work of contemplation deepens and rounds in step; the two clingings of self and Dharma are gradually transformed and removed; and Dharma and non-Dharma are gradually no longer clung to. It is as they say: when the water arrives, the channel forms — things one could not have expected simply come to be. Nor is it only that one comprehends Buddhist principle. This was spoken in terms of Dharma.

As for form and sound: where there are eyes there is seeing, and nothing seen is not form; where there are ears there is hearing, and nothing heard is not sound; fragrance, taste, and touch follow the same pattern. Even if one flees to a place where no one is, the bright moon among the mountains meets the eye and becomes form; the clear wind on the river meets the ear and becomes sound. How is one to keep far from them? You must know that if the mind is not pure, then even if one blocks one’s hearing and seals one’s sight, there is no telling how many phantom forms of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch appear within one’s mental realm. One must, as said above, advance in understanding and practice together, habituating oneself long, so that the eye of the Way becomes bright and the mind of the Way becomes pure, and one can reverse seeing and reverse hearing. Only then will such realms as form and sound no longer arise in the mind. Then, meeting objects and circumstances, one can see as though not seeing, hear as though not hearing.

You should further know that in speaking these two lines, “if the mind has abiding, then it is non-abiding,” the Buddha was addressing those who have resolved for bodhi and cultivate the bodhisattva path. For having made great compassionate vows to continue and exalt the Buddha-seed, wishing to save every living being and bring all to Buddhahood, one cannot forsake living beings life after life. If one is not apart from all marks, one will fear the round of birth and death, and one’s great mind of the Way will retreat. Moreover, if one does not forsake living beings, one cannot forsake dust-realms; and the moment realms are mentioned, there are favorable and adverse. If one cannot give rise to a non-abiding mind and be apart from all marks, then on meeting an adverse circumstance, can one fail to retreat? Thus Śāriputra made the great resolve and cultivated the great practice for sixty kalpas. Because a man begged for his eye, he dug out one eye; when the man then asked for the other, he retreated from the great and cultivated the small. This is clear proof. Should one meet favorable circumstances — become a king of men, a god, or Śakra — one must likewise be apart from marks. Only then will the mind of the Way be firm and not be turned by pleasant realms. Moreover, while a bodhisattva transforms below, he must still seek above. Our World-Honored One, through many kalpas, in deeds such as leaping into fire for a single line and giving up his body for half a verse, passed through we know not how many. All of this came from the power of being able to be apart from marks. For this reason one must assuredly not dwell in the six dusts and give rise to mind, and only then is one apart from all marks. When marks are left behind, the nature appears. When the nature appears, only then can one remain unmoved in the bodhimaṇḍa and manifest bodies throughout the dust-worlds, fulfilling the original bodhi vow to seek above and transform below. This is why the World-Honored One said it again and again.

Speaking from this point, is it not hard for one who makes the great resolve and cultivates the great practice? Yet there is a surpassing expedient, and what is hard becomes not hard. What is the expedient? Reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth in the West. You should know that the Dharma-door of Buddha-recitation and seeking rebirth was spoken precisely for those who make the great mind of the Way, and only incidentally for the rest. Worldly people do not know this and so belittle it — a great, great mistake! The Awakening of Faith says: “When living beings first learn this Dharma (referring to the great mind and great practice), wishing to seek right faith, their minds are timid and weak. Dwelling in this Sahā world, they fear of themselves that they cannot always meet the Buddhas, serve and make offerings to them in person, and dreading that faith may be hard to accomplish, they wish to retreat. They should know that the Tathāgata has a surpassing expedient to gather and protect their faith: namely, by the cause of single-minded Buddha-recitation, they may be born in other Buddha-lands according to their vows, always see the Buddha, and forever leave the evil paths. As a sūtra says: if a person single-mindedly recollects Amitābha Buddha of the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the West, and dedicates the roots of goodness he has cultivated toward rebirth in that world, he will attain rebirth. Because he always sees the Buddha, he will in the end never retreat. (The above is the expedient for those who do not know how to be apart from marks, that is, what was spoken for the rest.) If one contemplates that Buddha’s true-mark dharma-body (contemplating the dharma-body means precisely contemplating the nature apart from marks), and diligently cultivates it (the word cultivate here covers both being apart from marks and reciting the Buddha’s name), one will ultimately attain rebirth and dwell in right concentration. (Dwelling in right concentration is the accomplishment of the root of faith.)” Reading this passage of the treatise is enough to prove that the Dharma-door of Buddha-recitation and seeking rebirth was spoken precisely for those who make the great resolve. For wishing them to escape timidity and retreat, it opens this surpassingly excellent expedient Dharma-door. Drawing near Amitābha and dwelling in right concentration, one not only accomplishes the root of faith but has already partially realized the dharma-body. One can then manifest bodies in a hundred realms (this is said of the initial dwelling; from the initial dwelling upward it is a thousand realms, ten thousand realms, increasing tenfold and tenfold again) and save living beings widely. Whatever the circumstance, favorable or adverse, one meets it as though nothing were there. With such a surpassing expedient, why be timid and fail to make the great resolve? And one who has already made the great resolve — how can he not cultivate this method?

The treatise speaks of two forms of rebirth. (1) One who both recollects that Buddha and dedicates the various roots of goodness he has cultivated toward rebirth will attain rebirth and in the end never retreat. This is one who cannot yet be apart from marks and see the nature, but by relying on the power of the Buddha’s gathering and protection attains non-retreat. (2) One who both recollects that Buddha and can contemplate the Buddha’s true-mark dharma-body will ultimately attain rebirth and dwell in right concentration. This is one who can be apart from marks and contemplate the nature, and so, having attained rebirth, dwells in right concentration. To dwell in right concentration means one has already ascended to the initial dwelling. This is what is called top-grade rebirth: on arrival the flower opens, one sees the Buddha, and awakens to the patient acceptance of non-arising. Therefore, if we cultivate being apart from marks together with Buddha-recitation, relying on the protective mindfulness of our Original Teacher, the Guide who receives and leads us, and the Buddhas of the ten directions, then with one pushing and one pulling, sailing with the wind behind us, will there be any who do not swiftly reach the other shore? Then let no one neglect the method of cultivating prajñā and Pure Land together, spoken of earlier.

What the Awakening of Faith says about contemplating the Buddha’s true-mark dharma-body must not be read in a narrow way. The sutra says: mind, Buddha, and living beings — these three are without difference. Since one is apart from marks and contemplates the nature (to contemplate the dharma-body is the sense of contemplating the nature, and also the sense of being apart from marks), then to contemplate the Buddha’s dharma-body is to contemplate one’s own original nature — you should know it thus. Look carefully at this section gathering up the non-abiding resolve: it not only echoes the meaning in the opening answer on subduing, but also echoes the meaning in the answer on abiding (that is, the two great sections “should thus subdue his mind” and “should dwell on nothing in practicing giving”). The sense is very clear, and there is no need to set it out at length.

The meaning in the earlier answer on subduing is to cause one to make the great vow of being apart from marks. The meaning in the answer on abiding is to cause one to cultivate the great practice of being apart from marks. Together they are precisely the teaching that one should thus resolve. From this it is clear that the earlier text, on the surface, seems only to answer the questions on subduing and abiding; in fact it also answers the question on resolving. This meaning is brought to life and made clearer by the phrase here, “one should be apart from all marks in resolving for bodhi.” Again, this section gathering up the non-abiding resolve, though it gathers up all that was said since the sutra opened, only gathers up the gate of contemplation. Hence the next section specially speaks of giving, which is the practice that includes all six pāramitās within the gate of action. It not only gathers up the earlier meaning of non-abiding giving but also shows that the gates of contemplation and action are equally weighty and cannot be apart. And the reason contemplation is spoken first and action second is further to show that all practice should take the wisdom of contemplation as its guide. The principle is fine and strict, the exposition again skillful — one should quietly comprehend it.

It was said above that the earlier section on giving rise to the non-abiding mind is the gathering-point of all meanings spoken after the sutra opened, and that this present section gathering up the non-abiding resolve is the grand gathering-point. What is a gathering-point, and what is a grand gathering-point? Though the meaning has been explained, there remains something unsaid; let me add it here. For it is an essential meaning and cannot be left unknown. Otherwise, it might as well not be spoken at all.

In the earlier section on giving rise to the non-abiding mind, the phrase “should give rise to the pure mind” is the gathering-point of the various meanings of being apart from marks spoken after the sutra opened. Why? Because being apart from marks is originally for the sake of realizing the nature and causing the pure mind to appear; for if it does not appear, one cannot turn the ordinary into the noble. Hence “should give rise to the pure mind.”

The phrase “he should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing” is the gathering-point of the meanings of clinging to neither empty nor existent spoken after the sutra opened. Why? Because clinging to neither of the two extremes of empty and existent requires that calm and insight be applied together. For when one dwells on nothing, the mind is empty and still — this is called calm; when one gives rise to mind, the mind is bright and illumining — this is called insight. This is what the Chan school calls alert yet still, still yet alert. Thus concentration and wisdom are equal, and only then does one accord with the original nature that is empty as-it-is and not empty as-it-is. (In other words, only with equal concentration and wisdom can one cling to neither empty nor existent.) Only then can one realize the wonderful fruit of stillness and illumination simultaneous. Because Buddhas and bodhisattvas realize this wonderful fruit, they manifest bodies throughout the realms without ever coming or going, and without making a mental effort yet respond wonderfully without limit. This great function in fact comes from applying calm and insight together and clinging to neither empty nor existent at the time of cultivating the cause. Therefore one who resolves for bodhi should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing. The two words “should” are important: it means one must do so, and only then does one accord with the original nature and with the wonderful fruit. The two “should not” are also important: to dwell in dust and give rise to mind is to unite with dust and turn the back on enlightenment, and then neither the virtue of the nature nor the virtue of the fruit accords. (The two “should” and the two “should not” in this section should be viewed in the same way.) Following the thread along, when we reach this point it is again the grand gathering-point of the earlier meanings, because it has come down to the source. This meaning was spoken before, but only to the extent that cultivating the six pāramitās is the cause of realizing the fruit and resolving is the cause that initiates cultivation — that is only one aspect of the source. You should know that what is called the source is not confined to a single aspect, and so it must be supplemented.

The earlier section on requesting the name and the upholding had already come to cutting off thought. This section teaches the most intimate and most elementary method of cutting off thought; hence it is said to have come down to the source.

The earlier section on the first pāramitā makes clear that every dharma is prajñā, which is to say that one should be apart from marks in every dharma. The section on the pāramitā of patience makes clear that only by being apart from marks can one accomplish patience — but that only states the principle. This section again teaches the most intimate and most elementary method of being apart from marks; hence it is said to have come down to the source. For cutting off thought is the source of seeing the nature, and being apart from marks is again the source of cutting off thought. In sum, this section and the next both point directly to the essential gate of practice; they are not merely subtle and wonderful principles. If one takes them as principle alone, does one not betray the sutra’s intent? Understand the method of practice in this section, and the next section can be applied. So let us speak now from this section.

It speaks of resolving and of giving rise to mind — the words “resolve” and “give rise” are important. They refer to the moment of stirring thought and moving the mind. The word “mind” is more important still: the bodhi mind, the non-abiding mind, is the true mind; dwelling in dust and giving rise to mind is the deluded mind. One “should” and one “should not” point directly to the student’s need to comprehend at the source of mind and to contemplate at the moment thought stirs, so that he does not practice in confusion. Hence it is called most intimate, most elementary. For such an instruction causes one to employ the right wisdom of prajñā to remove deluded thoughts, so that the mind of confusion and disturbance gradually comes to rest — this is the entry-level work; hence most elementary. And practiced thus, it is very practical and progress comes easily. Why? Because one knows the cause of becoming ordinary and the road to becoming noble, and sets to work at the crucial juncture. Hence most intimate.

What is the cause of becoming ordinary? You should know that all living beings, from beginningless time, because they have not reached the one dharma-realm, are named unenlightened, also called fundamental ignorance. Because of ignorance and non-enlightenment, thought stirs. Once thought arises, the confronting marks of subject and object appear in the mind. Then discrimination and calculation of self and person and the like flourish from this. The more one clings, the more deluded; the more deluded, the more one clings. This is the cause of giving rise to delusion, creating karma, and receiving retribution — that is, the cause of becoming ordinary. Knowing this, one knows that there is no other road to becoming noble than to be apart from marks and still thought, thereby removing one’s discriminating clinging to self and person and the like. Why? Because where one falls, there one must rise.

To resolve for bodhi is to bring forth the initial mind of enlightenment. For bodhi means enlightenment. From beginningless time one has been unenlightened because one was deluded about the true and clung to marks. If now one does not know how to be apart from marks, what is meant by bringing forth enlightenment? Knowing this, the meaning of being apart from all marks and resolving for bodhi becomes clear. It is evident that this meaning is both lofty and near at hand. In its lofty aspect, one must reach wonderful enlightenment before marks are fully left behind. Yet the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition, and fruition penetrates to the source of the cause. So at the first arising of the resolve, one should thus know and thus learn. In its near aspect, clinging to marks means turning the back on enlightenment and uniting with dust — that is the cause of becoming ordinary; being apart from marks means turning the back on dust and uniting with enlightenment — that is the road to becoming noble. Therefore every student, at the moment thought stirs, should work earnestly at being apart from marks. It admits of no neglect.

Yet being apart from all marks is vast and all-encompassing — where is one to begin? The two lines “he should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form” and the rest point directly to the method of beginning. What is the method? The essential point is not to let phantom marks of form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas appear in the mind. When they appear, dismiss them; do not let them abide or cling. One should take the two words “should not” and hold them up with subtle and close attention. When a thought arises, one should raise the right thought and say: from beginningless time, because I dwelt in dust and gave rise to mind, greed and anger raced to arise, and I saw only self and no others, falling into evil paths beyond counting; even when born in a good path, I soon fell again; the suffering of rebirth is measureless and boundless. I suffered before without knowing it. Now by good fortune I have heard the Dharma and do know it — why should I still let it appear in my mind and not fear suffering? If I cannot even save myself, how can I benefit others? This is greatly improper. That is the first.

Again one should form the thought: to be deluded by marks is to be a living being; to be apart from marks is to be named a Buddha. One rises, one falls; one is noble, one is ordinary — all lies in a single turn of the mind. The interval admits not the breadth of a hair. Now that one studies Buddhism, at this hairbreadth juncture everything depends on deciding on the spot. Such phantom marks must absolutely not be allowed to linger in the mind. A moment’s indulgence and they are gone — what then is meant by studying Buddhism? This is greatly improper! That is the second.
Again one should form the thought: where has this come from now, that the mind is impure? This is greatly improper. That is the third.

You should know that where there is an object there is a subject. The phantom marks appearing in the mind are nothing other than what is born from the deluded thoughts that manifest them. So the reproach above directed at what appears, adding dismissal, is no different from reproaching the arising of the thought and adding dismissal. Thus to raise the right thought is to cut off deluded thoughts, like a sharp knife cutting through tangled hemp. Why? Because two thoughts cannot exist at the same time; when the right thought is raised, the deluded thought removes itself. From this we can see that calling these two lines the expedient for being apart from marks is precisely the expedient for being apart from thought. How intimate! To know to raise the right thought thus is to bring forth the initial mind of enlightenment. Hence it is called elementary.

The three thoughts given above go deeper layer by layer. (1) One takes the suffering of sinking into delusion as a warning. (2) One takes the striving for what is higher as a goad. (3) One turns the light back on the source of mind and causes it to tend toward original stillness. One may raise one thought, or several together, as the occasion allows. Working thus closely and densely at the moment thought stirs, one will have somewhat more assurance when meeting objects and circumstances.

Yet if the right thought is to be raisable at the moment thought stirs and the mind moves, one must also not relax at ordinary times — that is, when no thought has yet stirred. Hence it further says: “he should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing.” This line means that in ordinary times the mind should cling to nothing at all amid dust-realms. For this one should use the method spoken of earlier, cultivating prajñā and Pure Land together, as the expedient. Constantly let the mind be like empty space, pervading the dharma-realm, standing free beyond all confronting dust-realms. Then raise the single phrase of the Buddha’s name, so that Buddha and recitation blend like water and milk, and together with empty space and the dharma-realm become one great ocean of light. Simply recite straight on; when the mind grows the least dull or scattered, rouse it and gather it in.

That one should constantly let the mind equal empty space, pervade the dharma-realm, and stand beyond dust, is because the substance of the nature is itself thus, and because empty space, being markless, excludes nothing. Constantly practice this contemplation, letting this mind be open and void, and then Buddha-recitation will readily gain power. “Blending like water and milk” is what was called earlier not discriminating who is the reciter and who is the Buddha, but simply letting the recitation be the Buddha and there be no recitation apart from the Buddha. “Becoming one great ocean of light together with empty space and the dharma-realm” is because I and Amitābha are, together with the Buddhas of the ten directions and the living beings of the dharma-realm, of one single ocean of nature, without this or that, without difference. So now, reciting the Buddha’s name thus with one thought after another, thought after thought one’s light illumines that of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas above and shares their joy; and below one breathes in keeping with all living beings and shares in their reception. Thus thought after thought one seeks above, thought after thought one transforms below, and so together they become one great ocean of light.

Furthermore, since my mind and the Buddha’s mind are one single ocean of nature, one does not discriminate whether the Land of Ultimate Bliss is outside empty space and the dharma-realm or inside them, nor whether it is within the mind or outside it. Therefore together they become one great ocean of light. As for reciting straight on, it means not discriminating whether there are good signs or no good signs, whether one gains quick results or does not gain quick results. Simply press forward thus with nothing before one and recite in utmost sincerity.

One should further diligently raise the word “should,” to rouse oneself and not let slackness set in. Constantly form the thought: what mind have I resolved upon? Living beings await rescue most urgently; the Buddhas place their hopes on me most keenly. If I slacken even a little, then the resolve I made becomes a lie. Strive, strive! Taking this as a goad — this is the gate of “should.” If other thoughts arise, then according to the three kinds of right thought spoken of in the gate of “should not” above, one reproves and reproaches oneself. And one should earnestly hold up the two phrases “if the mind has abiding, then it is non-abiding,” closely and densely, never letting them be interrupted.

You should know that the arising of a thought is delusion, and the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name is likewise delusion, not the true. Why? Because the nature of true thusness is originally without thought. But because the deluded thoughts of ordinary beings never cease, one has no choice but to borrow the pure thought of Buddha-recitation to cure the deluded thoughts that dwell in dust. For though the thought of Buddha-recitation is not the substance of true thusness, it is the wonderful function that tends toward true thusness. Why? True thusness is the pure mind; the Buddha-thought is the pure thought. Both are pure, and so they accord. Therefore the thought of Buddha-recitation, unceasing thought after thought, can reach no-thought; hence it is called a surpassing expedient. Though this meaning was sketched before, because it is essential I have set it out thoroughly again.

The Land of Ultimate Bliss is likewise a phantom mark; yet one must seek and vow rebirth there, because a pure phantom is not the same as a defiled phantom. Why? Because a pure land is originally manifested by the pure mind. (This is what is meant by “when the mind is pure, the land is pure.” You should know that pure land and pure mind are originally non-dual; but in terms of receiving living beings, there is no way to name it, and so one is forced to name it a land.) There are many further meanings in seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, and they must be understood. Let me briefly state the most essential.

(1) In the position of an ordinary being, one should abandon the defiled and tend toward the pure. (The discriminating mind of ordinary beings is not yet removed. Without tending and abandoning, one cannot rouse oneself. This is precisely what was called earlier following along with the worldly principle of causality and confrontation, so as to plant the surpassingly unconditioned cause and attain the surpassingly unconditioned fruit. This is the wonderful function of the Buddha-Dharma. After being born in the Pure Land, one makes offerings to the Buddhas of other directions and saves living beings throughout the realms — how could one then abide in the marks of the Pure Land? Thus we know that causing one to abandon the defiled and tend toward the pure at the time of cultivating the cause is only a borrowed process for escaping the ocean of birth and death and fulfilling the bodhi vow.)

(2) To draw near Amitābha and accomplish the root of faith. (To cultivate from ordinary being up to the group of right concentration requires passing through countless kalpas. If one does not draw near a Buddha, one may truly fear a retreating mind. This is an important reason for seeking rebirth in the Pure Land.)

(3) To walk the bodhisattva path, one should manifest a pure land of adorned and wonderful marks in order to save the suffering living beings who are deluded and cling to marks. (One should manifest it — how then could seeking rebirth be an obstacle? Moreover, the seeking of rebirth now is precisely for the sake of swiftly realizing non-arising, and thereby being able to manifest boundless pure lands.)

(4) Neither extreme may be clung to. (Even all defiled phantoms should be met with clinging to neither empty nor existent — how much more so pure phantoms. For knowing that when the mind is pure the land is pure, one does not cling to the existent; and seeking Amitābha’s guidance, one does not cling to the empty. Why? Because without relying on the power of another Buddha, one’s own Buddha is not easily brought before one.)

(5) Having attained the substance, one should bring forth its function. (The two vehicles were reproached for having substance but no function. Therefore Mahāyāna cultivation should have substance and function complete. You should know that the meaning of seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, plainly put, is simply to realize the substance of the pure mind and bring forth the function of the pure land. For when all living beings see the auspicious signs of one’s rebirth, they will naturally give rise to faith. Thus in seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, within self-benefit there is already the function of benefiting others. Nor is it only after drawing near Amitābha that one can have the wonderful function of manifesting boundless pure lands.)

(6) The substance of the nature is empty and still, markless yet excluding no mark. (In reciting the Buddha’s name one must recite to the point of single-mindedness undistracted. Reaching this, one recites without reciting, and how could mind and land, defiled and pure, still be spoken of? This is marklessness. And at that very moment, Amitābha Buddha and the assembled sages appear before one — this is excluding no mark. From this one can awaken to the fact that the purport of Buddha-recitation and that of prajñā are not the least different.)

(7) Knowing that all is made by one mind, there is no obstruction. (Nature and marks are originally perfectly fused. Even defiled phantoms are no obstruction — how could pure phantoms be an obstruction? Whenever there is said to be an obstruction, it is because one does not know that all is made by the mind and so grasps at outer marks. If one knows this, then without clinging and without destroying, nature and marks are perfectly fused and all is unobstructed.)

All the above are most essential meanings of seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. Knowing these, one knows that Pure Land and prajñā, seeking rebirth and being apart from marks, differ in words but in meaning are truly not different. For prajñā, entering the Way through the gate of emptiness, is precisely the empty that is the existent; the Pure Land, entering the Way through the gate of the existent, is precisely the existent that is the empty. Seen together, this is precisely empty yet not empty, not empty yet empty. Therefore cultivating the two gates together precisely accords with the original nature that is empty as-it-is and not empty as-it-is. It is precisely the true marks that are markless yet exclude no mark. To set this aside and not seek it — is that not to wrong oneself?

Looking at the meaning of being apart from marks and apart from thought made clear above, we can see that if one would not dwell in the six dusts, there is no other way: the essential point is simply to dissolve marks and forget them. As for what was said earlier about keeping the essential lines and meanings of the sutra in the mind, steeping and savoring them — this is used to contemplate and dismiss clinging, what is called the method of using a phantom to remove a phantom; it is in no way at odds with dissolving marks and forgetting them. You should know that “should not dwell” and “dwell on nothing” only remove the illness, not the dharma. That is, form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch — offering to Buddhas, saving living beings, even nourishing this physical body — none of these can be abandoned or left unused. If one can avoid clinging, what obstruction is there? You should comprehend it thus.

The raising of the right thought spoken of above is extremely important. Fearing it may be overlooked, let me now explain the principle again. You should know that raising the right thought is precisely giving rise to mind; and raising the right thought is precisely what stills the deluded thoughts that abide in marks — it is precisely giving rise to a mind that dwells on nothing. It is named right thought because it comes from according with the principles spoken in the various Mahāyāna sutras. So to raise this right thought is itself the wisdom of contemplation. Possessing the light of this right contemplation, one can not only still deluded thoughts but also keep the mind from sinking — not comparable to using other methods without the wisdom of contemplation, where even if deluded thoughts are temporarily stilled, the mind is pitch dark within.

Someone may say: recitation is itself contemplation. Thus reciting the Buddha’s name or a mantra can both end birth and death and reveal the original nature. If it is as you have just said, are not Buddha-recitation and mantra-recitation both inferior to raising the right thought? The reply: your words seem right but are not. Because you know one point and miss ten thousand, taking a part for the whole, you have not fused and penetrated Buddhist principle. You should know that the esoteric school lays weight on the correspondence of the three mysteries, and the mystery of mind is precisely contemplation. If one merely recites a mantra without knowing how to contemplate, one can gain only small benefits; to seek the ending of birth and death and the revelation of the original nature will not be possible. So too with Buddha-recitation: one of top-grade rebirth must be unmoved in the mind of the supreme meaning, because he has the wisdom of contemplation. Otherwise one can only rely on the power of Amitābha’s reception to attain non-retreat and escape the round of rebirth. Only the Pure Land Dharma-door has this extraordinary expedient, which no other Dharma-door possesses. But if one wishes to see the original nature, one must first have the flower open and see the Buddha. And for the flower to open, one must first understand the supreme meaning and have wisdom arise. This is why those of middle and lower grade, after being born in the Pure Land, must still cultivate diligently for many dust-kalpas. From this one can awaken to the importance of the wisdom of contemplation.

That recitation is contemplation is certainly not wrong. But only when there is contemplation within the recitation can it be said that recitation is contemplation. And contemplation itself admits of the difference between contemplation of principle and contemplation of objects. Contemplation of principle means contemplating according to the principles spoken by the Buddha — such as the raising of the right thought described above. Since it is based on Buddhist principle, contemplating it can open one’s right wisdom; hence it is called the wisdom of contemplation. Contemplation of objects means contemplating according to objects. This again has two kinds. (1) Noble objects. (2) Dust objects. Contemplating noble objects means, in the Pure Land, contemplating the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the Buddha’s bodily marks and excellences, and what is spoken in the Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations. In the esoteric school, it means the contemplation of the maṇḍala, the contemplation of the dharma-realm, and the contemplation of the chosen deity — all these. Such noble objects are originally manifested by the pure mind, and so are non-dual with the pure mind; therefore contemplating them can still deluded thoughts and bring forth the true mind. As for the esoteric contemplation of the syllable A, this is contemplating the meaning of non-arising; it is contemplation of principle, not of objects. If one contemplates all dust objects, one must, according to what the Buddha taught, contemplate their impermanence and impurity and dismiss them — this is right contemplation, and also the wisdom of contemplation. Otherwise it is called wrong contemplation. Plainly put, one should not contemplate them. Such principles must not go unknown. Because the meanings of contemplating principle and contemplating objects interpenetrate, one who cultivates the esoteric school or the Pure Land, if he cannot contemplate according to his own school, should constantly raise the right thought to supplement it. He should further read much Mahāyāna to open the wisdom of contemplation, as was said earlier. This principle above all must not go unknown.

As for ordinary practice: if one cultivates prajñā alone, one may truly fear that one’s understanding of principle is not quite complete and that one falls into one-sided emptiness without knowing it. And there is the further fear that the mind is timid and weak, so that one may retreat without being aware. If one cultivates Buddha-recitation alone, not only will one’s grade of rebirth be low, but one may also fail to attain single-mindedness. Why? Because without knowing how to be apart from marks, one will surely dwell in the six dusts. With the mind disturbed by dust, how can there be single-mindedness? So it is best to cultivate being apart from marks and seeking rebirth together. Buddha-recitation is giving rise to mind; being apart from marks is dwelling on nothing. Though this mind is open and void, one raises the single phrase of the Buddha’s name — this is precisely giving rise to a mind that dwells on nothing. Nothing is more wonderful than this! Nothing is more secure than this!

It was said earlier that being apart from marks and seeking rebirth differ in words but not in meaning. The meaning of their non-difference can be made clear in a phrase: being apart from marks is also being apart from the marks of non-Dharma, and seeking rebirth is originally for the sake of realizing non-arising — how could they differ? Only, prajñā opens the gate of emptiness to cure the illness of clinging to the existent, and so speaks only of being apart from marks. The Pure Land opens the gate of the existent to cure the illness of one-sided emptiness, and so speaks only of seeking rebirth. This is why there is some difference in the words alone. Since being apart from marks and seeking rebirth are cultivated together, the expedients of practice and understanding spoken of earlier should still advance together at the same time. If on the side of understanding one gains the expedient, one can increase wisdom and nourish the mind of the Way. If on the side of practice one gains the expedient, then joy, anger, sorrow, and delight will perhaps not stir the master within, nor will one be pretentious and impatient, self-righteous and complacent. Otherwise the right thought will certainly not be raisable — never neglect this.

If all that has been said above is carried out one by one, is the work of practice then exhausted? Far, far from it! For though one may have assurance in stillness, in movement one may still be flustered. So besides practicing at ordinary times and at the moment thought stirs, one must further work when meeting objects and circumstances, passing through affairs to train the mind. Moreover, all that has been said above is only the cultivation of wisdom, not the cultivation of merit. You should know that wisdom is the guide and merit the rearguard. The great white ox-cart must have the two wheels of merit and wisdom to carry one to the other shore. If one does not cultivate merit, then having formed no karmic ties with living beings, one may become a bodhisattva yet be unable to receive and gather living beings. Moreover, if merit is not complete, then compassion is not complete. The bodhi mind takes great kindness and great compassion, self-enlightenment and enlightening others, equality without duality, as its root. If one does not cultivate the six pāramitās and all practices widely, the bodhi mind is already deficient, and the right wisdom of prajñā may not open either. Why? Because cultivating wisdom without cultivating merit still leaves the mark of self unremoved. Being neither equal nor compassionate, the Buddhas may not protect and mindful-remember one. Obstructions will surely multiply, so that one wishes to cultivate but cannot. This is why the next section again speaks of giving while not abiding.
(Yin) Second: Gathering up non-abiding giving. Two parts: (Mao) First, gathering up the “should not”; second, gathering up the “should.”
(Mao) First: Gathering up the “should not.”
“Therefore the Buddha says that the mind of a bodhisattva should not dwell in form when giving.”

The two words “therefore” carry on from the preceding text. Their tone closely follows “if the mind has abiding, then it is non-abiding.” Since abiding is wrong, the mind should not abide. This also gathers up the meaning from the opening of the sutra that one should not dwell in form, sound, and the rest when giving. The reason only the single phrase “should not dwell in form” is cited is that form means marks of form; raising the one word “form” already includes all realms and marks of affairs, and there is no need to enumerate them. The sense is as if to say: because abiding is wrong, therefore I said before that a bodhisattva should dwell on nothing in regard to dharmas when practicing giving, and should not dwell in form and the rest when giving. This instructs the hearer of the Dharma to take the meaning “if the mind has abiding, then it is non-abiding” and use it to verify what was said at the opening of the sutra; then its meaning becomes clear of itself.

Citing only the single phrase “should not dwell in form when giving” carries deep meaning besides. For form is precisely marks. Raising this makes it echo the earlier passage that one should be apart from all marks in resolving for bodhi. It lets one know that what is called being apart from marks means being apart from the marks of form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas that one clings to in the mind — it does not mean being apart from the dharmas of giving and the six pāramitās. At the opening of the sutra it was said that one should not dwell in form when giving, and there was originally no word “mind.” Here the word “mind” is specially added, again echoing the several instances of “mind” above. It lets one understand clearly that resolving for bodhi is resolving for the mind of the six pāramitās. And it lets one understand clearly that the reason one should not dwell in the six dusts and give rise to mind is precisely in order to practice giving and the six pāramitās. Then it is clear that the mind’s not dwelling in dust is by no means sinking into emptiness and stagnating in stillness. This is why earlier it spoke both of not abiding and of giving rise to mind, and said one should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing. One can understand even more clearly that since the mind does not dwell in dust precisely in order to practice the six pāramitās widely, then when practicing the six pāramitās the mind should likewise not dwell in dust. This is why the present text again says: “he should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing.” With this one phrase, all the meanings spoken before become interwoven and crisscrossed, pierced through in seven ways and eight. The World-Honored One spoke thus for no other purpose than to let the hearer of the Dharma fuse and penetrate them, deeply understand the purport, and thereby gain benefit in contemplation.

In sum, “the mind of a bodhisattva should not dwell in form when giving” follows closely upon “where there is abiding there is wrongness.” And the phrase “where there is abiding there is wrongness” was originally a reversal revealing that one should be apart from marks in resolving. So this section too serves to expound the meaning of resolving while apart from marks. For apart from giving and the six pāramitās there is no bodhi mind to be resolved. If the mind dwells at all in such marks as form and dust, the mind has already been turned by objects, and the practices of giving and the rest can certainly not be perfected. Can that still be called resolving for bodhi? Therefore one should not dwell in the six dusts but be apart from all marks; only then can one practice the six pāramitās widely, benefit all living beings, and perfect the bodhi resolve one has made. The next section, “the bodhisattva, for the benefit of all living beings, and so on,” unfolds this point fully. The two words “the Buddha says” also carry deep meaning. “Buddha” is a name for the virtue of fruition; when a bodhisattva’s practice is complete he is named a Buddha. If one would know the road down the mountain, one must ask one who has come that way. Here it says “the Buddha says,” so that one may know that the mind’s not dwelling in form when giving is the talk of experience, not an ideal. One who makes the great resolve should thus believe, understand, and uphold it. “Bodhisattva” refers to one who has resolved for bodhi; “bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas” at the opening of the sutra is the earlier instance.

Having spoken to this point, there is a further essential meaning that must not go unclarified. What is it? The Elder asked how one should abide, and the World-Honored One answered that one should dwell on nothing — what was His intent in this?
