As for non-abiding being the main purport of this sutra, and non-abiding meaning being apart from marks, and being apart from marks meaning realizing the nature, such principles have been fully set out above. What, then, is His intent here? It is spoken with direct reference to the sense of the question.

The Elder’s question had in mind obtaining a way for his mind to rest securely. And the World-Honored One no sooner opened His mouth than He said: “he should dwell on nothing.” This is simply answering something other than what was asked. Could it be that there is no such way at all? Or that the question should not have been asked? No. It is not that He answered something other than what was asked; it is a wonderful answer that does not answer. Why? Because dwelling on nothing at all is precisely the wonderful way to set the mind at rest. How is this shown to be so? Dwelling in neither Dharma nor non-Dharma is being apart from all marks. Being apart from all marks is not being turned by objects. Not being turned by objects, the mind rests securely and unmoved. Is this not a wonderful answer that answers without answering?

Yet though He did not answer in explicit words, earlier He said, “he should only abide as taught,” and now He says, “if the mind has abiding, then it is non-abiding.” One positive and one negative have already let slip much of where His intent lies. When I explained the meaning of “abide as taught” earlier, I said: it is abiding without abiding, that is, abiding in non-abiding. These two sayings make clear that at the very time when marks are not abided in, the mind is resting securely. Hence “abiding without abiding, abiding in non-abiding” is not a vague and boundless saying. When I explained “then it is non-abiding” earlier, I also said: it is not abiding as taught. For because one cannot abide in the non-abiding as taught and instead dwells in the six dusts, one’s mind is not resting securely and unmoved; hence “then it is non-abiding.” Since it is non-abiding, the contemplation of non-abiding has already been broken, and the giving and other practices one cultivates can certainly not be vast and boundless. Therefore this section closely follows that meaning and states it plainly: “Therefore the Buddha says that the mind of a bodhisattva should not dwell in form when giving.” Exceedingly pointed, exceedingly awakening. In sum, it makes clear that in resolving, in contemplating, and in practicing, all that was taught above is that one should dwell on nothing and be apart from all marks. For otherwise the mind unites with dust and does not rest securely, and the resolve one has made, the contemplation one practices, and the conduct one cultivates all become empty words. This is the true meaning of the Buddha’s answer, “he should dwell on nothing.” Now, taking the convenience of this passage, I have set it out thoroughly.

What was not said above was out of deference to the Buddha’s hidden intent. You should know that only when one dwells on nothing at all does one attain what to abide in. Only when one dwells on nothing from first to last does the dharma-body abide permanently. And one should not abide even in the dharma-body; hence it is said one does not abide in nirvāṇa. Because the small vehicle abides in nirvāṇa, it is called nirvāṇa with residue. So one must not abide even in nirvāṇa — that is entering nirvāṇa without residue. From this we can know that if one hears of “what to abide in” and gives rise to the thought of abiding, one will in the end never attain abiding. This is why the Buddha did not answer explicitly. Otherwise, why did He not say earlier, “he should only, as taught, attain the resting of the mind” — would that not be far clearer? Yet He only touched the word “abide” ever so lightly and would not speak it to the end, for no other reason than that living beings cling everywhere, and hearing of abiding they will give rise to the thought of abiding. Therefore those who expound sutras, in such places, should also defer to the Buddha’s hidden intent and not speak lightly. Yet this meaning cannot remain forever secret. So when the World-Honored One answered about abiding, though He did not say it explicitly, He pointed it out elsewhere. There are three places in all before and after. Two of them are clearest in sense. As was said above: only by being apart from marks can one be patient. And at the end of the sutra: “not grasping at marks, unmoved as thusness.” Patience and unmovedness are both meanings of resting securely. One must be apart from marks, and only then is it possible. Is this not the meaning that when marks are not abided in, the mind rests securely? So now I have set it out thoroughly as well, so that you may know the questions and answers truly meet point to point. One should quietly comprehend the Buddha’s profound intent: dwell on nothing at all, dwell on nothing from first to last.

The Second Patriarch of the Chan school asked for the method of setting the mind at rest. The First Patriarch said: “Bring me your mind, and I will set it at rest for you.” He said: “I seek the mind and cannot find it at all.” The First Patriarch said: “I have set your mind at rest for you.” This is exactly the same in sense as the questions and answers of this sutra. You should know that “he should dwell on nothing” is because the mind cannot be found at all. If one understands that it cannot be found at all, then the mind is set at rest.

In his treatise on the Diamond Sutra, Bodhisattva Asaṅga brought this meaning to life. For example, in explaining the section on subduing the mind, he says it is “for the sake of benefit, the profound mind abides,” also called “the resolve-mind abides.” In explaining the section on practicing giving while dwelling on nothing, he says it is “the pāramitā-corresponding practice abides.” This is precisely how the bodhisattva, deeply understanding the purport, dared to speak thus. In the treatise he does not say “the abiding gives rise to the profound mind” or “the abiding corresponds in practice,” but places the word “abide” after them — the meaning is very fine. It makes clear that only by cultivating non-abiding do the profound mind one has resolved upon and the corresponding practice one cultivates attain what to abide in. Now, taking this occasion, I have cited and explained it. If a reader of this treatise misunderstands it as clinging to giving rise to the profound mind and to the corresponding practice, he greatly violates the sutra’s intent, and it is by no means the treatise’s meaning either. From this we can know that the Great Prajñā Sutra’s saying “not abiding in any dharma is itself abiding in prajñā” also makes clear the meaning that when all dharmas are not abided in, the right wisdom of prajñā rests securely and unmoved. Otherwise it could not say that not abiding in anything is itself abiding. The meaning of the following line, “not believing in any dharma is named believing in prajñā,” is deeper still. To believe means not to waver. Not to waver means to rest securely. This makes clear that even resting securely is not abided in — and that is named resting securely. In such places, a hairsbreadth of difference leads a thousand miles astray. One must not merely stick to the words before one’s eyes; one should view the whole purport and quietly comprehend it. Hence the earlier saying that only by fusing all meanings can one penetrate a single meaning.
(Mao) Second: Gathering up the “should.” Two parts: (Chen) First, general statement; second, detailed explanation.
(Chen) First: General statement.
“Subhūti, the bodhisattva, for the benefit of all living beings, should thus practice giving.”

The preceding section said one should not dwell in form when giving; fearing that those who fail to grasp the meaning might misunderstand it as meaning only that one should not dwell in the existent, He therefore spoke the several sections that follow, so that one may know this is not dwelling in either the empty or the existent.
In the circulating editions, after “all living beings” there is an extra word “therefore.” All the ancient editions lack it.

The two words “thus” point to what follows. The word “for” is read in the departing tone, and it is important. For one is named a bodhisattva because he has resolved for bodhi. And for what purpose has he resolved for bodhi? For the benefit of all living beings. Since he resolves for the benefit of all, he should practice giving as stated below. Why? Because if he does not give, what benefit is there for others? And if he does not do as stated below, how is it the pāramitā of giving? Then he could not benefit even a few living beings, much less all living beings. Could it still be said that he resolves for bodhi for the benefit of all living beings? This is why the sutra says at the opening that if there are the four marks of self and person, one is not a bodhisattva. This is enough to prove that after “all living beings” there truly is no word “therefore.” For one is named a bodhisattva precisely because he can resolve for the benefit of all living beings; if the word “therefore” were added, then being a bodhisattva would be one thing and benefiting all living beings another, and the sense would go slack altogether.
“For the benefit of all living beings, he should thus practice giving” contains two meanings:

(1) He should practice giving as stated below, being apart from marks. For only giving while apart from marks can receive and gather living beings without measure or bound and benefit them all. This is the same in sense as the opening of the sutra: “I shall cause all living beings without number, without measure, without bound to enter extinction.” Yet at the opening it was to cause one to make the great vow to benefit all living beings, so as to be apart from the marks of self and person. Here it is to cause one to be apart from the marks of the giver, the gift, and the rest, so as to accomplish the original vow to benefit all living beings. The two meanings before and after assist each other, and neither can be lacking.

(2) He should give all living beings the Dharma as stated below, so that all may cultivate both merit and wisdom and benefit one another in turn, and all may know to be apart from all marks and become bodhisattvas and Buddhas. Giving thus is true benefit. This is the original intent of one who resolves, and also the original intent of the Buddha’s teaching. Why? Because among all gifts the gift of Dharma is supreme. This is the same in sense as the opening of the sutra: “all classes of living beings, I shall cause them all to enter nirvāṇa without residue.” Yet at the opening it only caused one to make the vow to save living beings and bring them to Buddhahood. Here it causes one to actually practice the Dharma-gift of saving living beings and bringing them to Buddhahood. It also supplies what was not covered in the earlier statement, “he should dwell on nothing in practicing giving.” In sum, this conclusion gathers up the two great sections of the preceding text, in each case expounding what was said before and making it more complete. Hence the heading says “gathering up.”

Giving is the practice of forsaking oneself for the benefit of others. In the Buddha-Dharma, not only giving benefits others; every gate of practice has benefiting others as its sole purport. So citing giving alone includes every gate of practice. You should know that the main purport of this sutra lies in non-abiding. The main purport of non-abiding lies in dismissing clinging and breaking the self. And forsaking oneself for the benefit of others is the sharp knife and keen axe for dismissing clinging and breaking the self. Therefore in contemplation it unfolds non-abiding, and in practice it singles out giving — to show that the two gates of contemplation and practice must correspond and complete each other. One must uphold it thus, and only then does one resolve for bodhi and realize the fruit of bodhi.

A bodhisattva’s resolve is originally to save himself and others, benefiting both. Yet at the opening of the sutra He only caused one to save all living beings, without speaking of saving oneself. Here too He speaks only of the bodhisattva benefiting all living beings, without speaking of self-benefit — this carries deep meaning. This meaning was spoken before, but there is no harm in saying it again to make it clear. You should know that the reason living beings are living beings is that they cling to self and to marks. So in resolving and practicing, one should keep only the mind of saving others and the vow to benefit the many, in order to break the beginningless illness of clinging to self and marks. This is precisely the essential gate for turning the ordinary into the noble. Hence self-saving and self-benefit are not spoken of, yet self-saving and self-benefit are already within. In other words, saving others is precisely how one saves oneself, and benefiting the many is precisely how one benefits oneself. The wonderful function of the Buddha-Dharma lies exactly here. Every Buddhist principle should be comprehended thus: if one is taught only to dwell on nothing, then one’s mind rests in patience, unmoved as thusness, and it is thereby accomplished. If one is only made to see through the five aggregates and this physical body and to remove greed, anger, and delusion, then the physical body thereby becomes healthy and at ease. If one is only made to cultivate world-transcending dharmas, then worldly dharmas thereby become daily better governed. For if most people can know to resolve for bodhi and walk the bodhisattva path, the highest may turn the ordinary into the noble, the middling become greatly benevolent and wise, and the lowest become good people and gentlemen. Then the prosperity of the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns spoken of in the books would not surpass it. Yet those without faith all take it for world-weariness, and even the faithful think it has nothing to do with worldly dharmas — there is no greater betrayal of the Buddha’s kindness than this. All of this is the fault of not understanding Buddhist principle. Therefore one who makes the great resolve and wishes to spread the Buddha-Dharma should first proclaim this meaning with all his strength and expound it thoroughly, so that the multitude may gradually come to understand and many may enter the Buddha’s gate. Then to transform the whole world into a realm of great harmony and the whole dharma-realm into a land of ultimate bliss would not be difficult. I wish to encourage you all in this. In sum, the Buddha-Dharma always says that speaking of this side includes that side, and doing that side is accomplishing this side. Not only does it work both ends at once, it is perfectly complete on every side. Hence it is said that all the good words in the world were spoken to the end by the Buddha. Hence at the Avataṃsaka assembly the great bodhisattvas praised Him, saying: “In heaven and on earth there is none like the Buddha; throughout the worlds of the ten directions there is no equal. All that exists in the world I have fully seen; there is nothing at all that equals the Buddha.”
(Chen) Second: Detailed explanation.
“The Tathāgata says: all marks are precisely non-marks; and again He says: all living beings are precisely non-living beings.”

Marks are not marks; living beings are not living beings. This is exactly the same in sense as the earlier saying that the mark of self is precisely non-mark, and the rest. What is said here is to cause one who walks the bodhisattva path to know that all marks and all living beings, at the very time they exist, are precisely the time they are empty. This is what is called the existent being precisely the empty, and the empty being precisely the existent. One should thus be apart from both extremes of empty and existent. Only then can one benefit all living beings. “The Tathāgata says” is spoken with respect to the nature. The nature is itself empty and existent at once. And all marks and all living beings are never apart from this nature of one substance; they are all manifested by this nature of one substance. Hence none of them is not existent-as-empty and empty-as-existent. The meaning that the existent is precisely the empty and the empty is precisely the existent has been repeatedly stated. Yet since this is the main meaning of prajñā, unless it is thoroughly understood, no Buddhist principle can be understood, and all gates of contemplation and practice and all kinds of cultivation can gain no power. So now I will analyze and explain it in greater detail.

You should know that no dharma is anything but a provisional present mark at the time when causes and conditions gather. So when conditions gather it arises, and when conditions scatter it perishes. Nor need one wait for it to perish to know this. Even while it is gathered and present, it is constantly changing, impermanent and unfixed; from this one can understand that it is not solid and firm but is in truth a phantom, provisional mark. This is what is called the existent being precisely the empty. But ordinary beings who do not understand this principle mistake it for real, and so grasp at existent marks and drift along with them. This is the cause of rebirth. The Buddha’s eye, seeing through this point and knowing that all dharmas are existent-as-empty, therefore bids one not cling to the existent. And He further knows that the reason all dharmas have such various and different marks is that they differ according to the power of karma. Because the karma one creates changes at every moment, the marks of the realm likewise change and are impermanent. Yet whatever cause one makes, precisely such a fruit appears. The beauty or ugliness, suffering or joy of all the marks of the realm differ according to the goodness or evil, greatness or smallness of one’s karma. When karma is complex, the marks that appear are complex; when karma is pure, the marks that appear are pure. There is not the slightest deviation. This is what is called the empty being precisely the existent. But ordinary beings who do not understand this principle deny causality, and so grasp at empty marks and do anything at all. This is the cause of falling. Even if not, and one takes the one-sided emptiness of the small vehicle, then again there is substance but no function. The Buddha’s eye, seeing through this point and knowing that all dharmas are empty-as-existent, therefore bids one not fall into one-sided emptiness.

Nor is that all. He further knows from where karma arises: it arises from the having of thoughts in the mind. And a thought must have a root: it is rooted in the nature we all share. Thoughts and karma change at every moment; only this shared spiritual nature, from beginningless time to the end of the future, neither changes nor differs, and is in truth the main substance of all dharmas. Yet where there is substance there must be function, and where there is function there must be marks. This is why marks, though phantom-existent, are never interrupted. Because they are phantom yet uninterrupted, one should cling neither to the existent nor to the empty. And since one knows that marks turn with karma and karma is made in the mind, one knows that though the cause of a single thought is subtle, its connections are exceedingly great. This is why the student is bid to contemplate and work at the moment thought stirs. One further knows that the arising of thoughts is due to not having reached the one true dharma-realm, and so one grasps at marks and discriminates. Yet the substance of the nature is originally without thought. If one does not turn the light back on the source of mind, how can one cut off thought and realize the substance? This is why the student is bid to turn the back on dust and unite with enlightenment, to reverse delusion and return to the true.

The profound and subtle principles above — who could know them without the Buddha’s instruction? And if one does not believe the Buddha and uphold them according to the Dharma, who could understand them? Therefore all living beings, from ancient times to the present, mostly dwell in delusion, create karma, and suffer. So one who resolves for bodhi for the benefit of all living beings should know that marks are precisely non-marks and beings are precisely non-beings; clinging neither to the existent nor to the empty, thus apart from both empty and existent, he practices the six pāramitās and all practices. Only then can he benefit all living beings. Why? Because giving while dwelling in marks easily causes the mind of the Way to retreat. Clinging to the existent is dwelling in marks, and clinging to the empty is likewise dwelling in marks; hence one should be apart from both. One should further proclaim this principle — that marks are precisely non-marks and beings precisely non-beings — to all living beings, so that all may know to cultivate the cause of being apart from both extremes and realize the fruit of stillness and illumination simultaneous. This is the ultimate benefit, and the bodhisattva should thus practice giving. This section opens with “the Tathāgata says,” precisely to point out that one who makes the great resolve should thus be apart from both empty and existent in practicing giving, and should give this wonderful Dharma of being apart from both empty and existent. Then self and others alike are apart from marks and see the nature, cut off thought and realize the substance, and together return to the ocean of nature. The greatness of its benefit is inconceivable. Why? Because it is the Tathāgata who says it, and because that Dharma accords with the Tathāgata’s virtue of nature.

“All marks” and “all living beings” have many kinds of meaning. Past books have mostly taken one or two meanings as the text allowed and explained them. If one does not know their many meanings, one understands only that it is so, not why it is so; and then, because the books one has seen differ, contradictions may arise. Let me now gather all the meanings and analyze and explain them in detail. Then hearing this one session will be worth ten years of reading — something I imagine you would wish to hear. Among these many meanings some are common, some uncommon, and some are extensions; they may be summarized in the four heads below.

(1) Marks means appearances — the appearances of living kinds. The word “marks” refers not only to outward appearances but also to inner conditions. Living kinds are, as the sutra says at the opening, those born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; those with form or without form; those with thought, without thought, or neither with nor without thought. The formless class has only no karma-fruit form; it still has a subtle form-body manifested by the fruition of concentration. Because it cannot be seen by the eye below the form realm, it is called formless — yet the Buddha’s eye, the bodhisattva’s Dharma-eye, and the arhat’s wisdom-eye can all see it. When the World-Honored One showed his entry into nirvāṇa, the gods of the formless realm wept tears like rain. Had they no form-body, how could tears fall? Such various living kinds differ endlessly in the marks of their form and mind; hence “all marks.” Distinguish further: within each class the appearances differ in many ways, such as outward fatness or thinness, beauty or ugliness, and inward goodness or evil, wisdom or folly. Extending this, as the Chapter on Vows and Conduct says, with all their varied life-spans, varied desires and delights, varied mental conduct, and varied demeanors, they are a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions, beyond all reckoning; hence “all.” Yet all such marks, while they seem plainly present to the ordinary eye, are seen by the eye of the Way to be nothing but the false union of form, feeling, conception, formations, and consciousness, the five aggregates, manifesting various marks of living kinds. Apart from what the five aggregates manifest, no such differing marks can be found at all. This is why the sutra says that at this very moment they are empty, and again that arising is non-arising. Hence “all marks are precisely non-marks.” (Read the second line with emphasis; the same applies below and to the second head.) This makes clear the meaning of the emptiness of beings. Since this is spoken with respect to the appearances of living kinds, that arising is non-arising, it is called the emptiness of beings.

As for “living beings”: “beings” means the five aggregates. Three makes a multitude; since the aggregates are five, it is named a multitude. Through the false union of the many dharmas of the five aggregates there is then birth; hence “living being.” And the living beings of the four modes of birth (womb, egg, moisture, transformation) and the six paths (gods, humans, asuras, hells, hungry ghosts, animals) are all born through the false union of these five aggregates; hence “all living beings.” The common meaning of “living beings” refers to the thousand-fold multitude of living kinds. This is the meaning of “all living beings,” not the original meaning of the two words themselves. What is the false union of the five aggregates? You should know that not only are living kinds a union of the dharmas of the five aggregates, falsely appearing as the mark of birth and originally unreal; the many dharmas of the five aggregates themselves are likewise unions of other many dharmas, falsely appearing as this phantom mark, and are likewise originally unreal. Hence “the false union of the five aggregates.” How so? Take the aggregate of form: it is manifested by the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind. So the aggregate of form is clearly a false union. And if one examines closely, which of the four great elements is not false? As for the four aggregates of feeling, conception, formations, and consciousness: feeling is reception, conception is recollection, formations is flowing change, consciousness is discrimination and retention — all are the deluded mind. What is the deluded mind? Because from beginningless time it has been various calculations and various clingings, accumulating countless karmic forces, holding them without interruption, and thereby manifesting the various activities of feeling, conception, formations, and consciousness. In the pure mind of self-nature, where could such a thing be? So the false union of these four aggregates is likewise clear. Thus not only is the multitude of the five aggregates originally no multitude; the other many dharmas that falsely unite to form the five aggregates are also multitude yet not multitude. Then that birth is originally non-birth is perfectly evident. This is why the sutra says that the very substance is empty. Hence “all living beings are precisely non-living beings.” This makes clear the meaning of the emptiness of dharmas. Since this is spoken with respect to the many dharmas of the five aggregates, that the very substance is empty, it is called the emptiness of dharmas. From this we can see how exquisite the meaning of the two words “five aggregates” is. “Aggregate” means gathering, and also covering. It makes clear that form, feeling, conception, formations, and consciousness are what other many dharmas gather into, and that living kinds are again what these five gather into — precisely what is called arising through the gathering of conditions. And all living beings, deluded about all marks because from beginningless time they have long been covered and obscured by them, come to cling and take them as real, creating karma and suffering without measure or bound. Now that one knows this, one should break this obscuration and leap out of the cage. How to break it? By relying on this Diamond Prajñā’s being apart from marks and dismissing clinging. For making clear the emptiness of beings serves to break the clinging to self and be apart from the mark of self; making clear the emptiness of dharmas serves to break the clinging to dharmas and be apart from the mark of dharmas. And the moment dharmas are spoken of, non-dharmas are included. Why? Because clinging to non-dharma is also clinging to dharma; for in the mind of the one who clings, non-dharma is taken as dharma. So the moment one speaks of being apart from the mark of dharmas, the meaning of being apart from the mark of non-dharmas must be included as well. To speak thus is to speak as the Buddha spoke; to know thus is right knowledge. Then even emptiness is emptied. The emptiness of beings, the emptiness of dharmas, and the emptiness of emptiness — these are the three emptinesses. The right wisdom possessing these three emptinesses is named Diamond Prajñā. Therefore one who makes the great resolve must not only understand the meanings of the emptiness of beings and the emptiness of dharmas in order to be apart from the two marks of self and Dharma and thereby break this obscuration and leap out of the cage; he must also understand the meaning of the emptiness of emptiness in order to be apart from the mark of non-dharma and thereby benefit all living beings. So if a bodhisattva’s mind penetrates that marks are not marks, then though marks exist the mind is empty. Since he is no longer caged by marks, he may well manifest all marks and save all living beings deluded by marks, without giving rise to timidity. And if he further penetrates that living beings are not living beings, he knows that the nature of living beings is originally empty and still, the same as the Buddha’s. So he vows to save all into nirvāṇa without residue, yet has no thought that living beings are hard to save; and even having saved all living beings, he has no thought that any living being has been saved. Why? Because beings are originally no beings and birth is originally non-birth. Only thus is one a bodhisattva who has resolved for the benefit of all living beings.

(2) The meaning that living beings are not living beings, as stated in the first head, is used to prove the meaning that marks are not marks. For if one knows that the many dharmas of the five aggregates are themselves manifested by other many dharmas, it is evident that the five aggregates are provisional dharmas. Then are not all marks manifested by the five aggregates provisional dharmas within provisional dharmas? That they are existent yet non-existent is clear. Hence “all marks are precisely non-marks.” These two lines, then, also make clear the meaning of the emptiness of dharmas. And if one knows that the five-aggregate form-body of every living being is gathered by the four great elements and held by karmic force, and that in the pure mind none of this exists, then one can awaken to the fact that in terms of what the five aggregates manifest, marks indeed differ from one another, but in terms of the pure mind of self-nature, there is no difference and no mark. How then could one be blind to the true nature of one substance and cling to the phantom marks of birth, discriminating self, person, and living being? Hence “all living beings are precisely non-living beings.” These two lines, then, make clear the meaning of the emptiness of beings. Joined with the first head, “marks are precisely non-marks” directly makes clear the emptiness of beings and also makes clear the emptiness of dharmas; and “beings are precisely non-beings” directly makes clear the emptiness of dharmas and also makes clear the emptiness of beings.

(3) Marks means the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of living being, and the mark of life. The four marks are not one, hence “all marks.” Whether one clings to the mark of body, the mark of Dharma, or the mark of non-Dharma, all are clinging to self, person, living being, and life; hence “all.” And the mark of body is the false union of the five aggregates; the five aggregates are already unreal. Dharma and non-Dharma are even more mere provisional names. Yet there are not no such marks of provisional name and unreality. Hence “all marks are precisely non-marks.” (Read the first line with emphasis; the same applies below.) This makes clear the meaning of the three emptinesses — the emptiness of beings, of dharmas, and of emptiness. This meaning should be spoken with respect to the giver. Hence the opening of the sutra says: “a bodhisattva should dwell on nothing in regard to dharmas when practicing giving.” And again: “he should thus practice giving, not dwelling in marks.” It is said over and over to show that neither extreme is dwelt in. “All living beings” is still as in the first and second explanations. Yet though beings are originally no beings and birth is originally non-birth, though beings are empty and dharmas are empty, since they are falsely united and manifested by the dharmas of the five aggregates, there are not no phantom marks of living beings. Hence: “all living beings are precisely non-living beings.” This too makes clear the meaning of the three emptinesses. This meaning should be spoken with respect to the receiver of the gift. For it is the phantom-marked living beings who are obscured by the false dharmas of the five aggregates and do not know that these are false and not real. So here the bodhisattva who resolves for the benefit of all living beings is told to practice giving widely by the prajñā Dharma-door of the existent being precisely the empty and the empty being precisely the existent.

(4) “All marks” means the giver and the gift. “All” because the giver is a union of the five aggregates and the gifts are of many kinds. “All living beings,” as explained above, means the receivers. Whether giver, gift, or receiver, none is anything but the gathering of causes and conditions manifesting this phantom existence; hence all are called non-. This is what is called the three wheels being empty of substance. A wheel is a thing that turns without rest, used to figure giver, gift, and receiver benefiting one another in turn without cease. “Empty of substance” has two meanings: (1) These three are all phantom existent, empty in their very substance. (2) These three are phantom existent in their mark and substance, but empty and still in the substance of their nature. If one understands the meaning that the very substance is empty, one can avoid clinging to marks; if one understands the meaning that the substance of the nature is empty and still, one should return to the nature. One who makes the great resolve and can give thus — his benefit is vast and great.

All four explanations above serve to make clear the meaning that the existent is precisely the empty and the empty is precisely the existent. The earlier words “he should thus practice giving” mean that one who understands non-marks and non-beings does not stagnate in the existent; and one who understands that marks are precisely non-marks and beings precisely non-beings does not fall into the empty. Because he does not stagnate in the existent, he gives yet does not abide; because he does not fall into the empty, he does not abide yet constantly gives. Since he clings to neither extreme and applies both wheels together, this is the pāramitā of giving. Therefore the bodhisattva should thus cultivate the three kinds of giving that are precisely marks yet apart from marks, benefiting all living beings who are non-arising yet phantom-arising.

This section not only explains and establishes the earlier meaning that one should not dwell in form and the rest when giving, which is not dwelling in either empty or existent; it also echoes the various meanings spoken earlier, unfolds them, and concludes them. For it was said above: whatever has marks is all delusive — because all marks are precisely non-marks. And it was said: if one sees that marks are not marks, one sees the Tathāgata. And again: one who is apart from all marks is named a Buddha. So now it says one should thus be precisely marks yet apart from marks in practicing giving. Practicing thus, one saves oneself and others, together sees the Tathāgata, and is named a Buddha; hence “for the benefit of all living beings.” You should know that this phrase includes the giver as well. Why? Because the giver himself is also one of the living beings. Moreover, the earlier statements about giving without dwelling in marks and about there being in truth no living being who attains extinction also become clearer in meaning on this account. Why? What was said before about giving without dwelling in marks was immediately followed by the explanation of merit; and what was said about no living being attaining salvation stated only that it is so. Now, one by one, the why of it is unfolded. For marks being precisely non-marks, it is evident that there is originally nothing to abide in, and so one should not abide. And beings being precisely non-beings, it is evident that living beings entering nirvāṇa without residue are only recovering their original nature, and so there is no one who is saved. In sum, with these two concluding sections, all the meanings spoken before are rounded to completion. Therefore these two concluding sections of sutra text should be engraved on one’s inmost heart, morning and evening, diligently savored — they hold great benefit.

When practicing giving and the other practices, one should, as in the earlier section gathering up the non-abiding resolve, constantly form right thoughts according to the principle of the gate of “should,” as a goad. If one clings even slightly to the six dusts, one should, as in the earlier gate of “should not,” constantly raise the right thought and reproach oneself. If one leans even slightly toward emptiness, one should, according to what is said here, raise the right thought and say: benefiting living beings is my original vow — why am I slack, seeking only my own salvation? This itself is clinging to self. The view of self is the root from which delusion arises; if this root is not removed, how can one save oneself? One should further constantly contemplate that whatever has marks is empty and existent at once; that living beings are kin and kin are living beings; that living beings are of one substance; and that living beings are originally Buddhas.

Though contemplation and practice open two gates, in fact they correspond and complete each other. Consider that in the earlier gate of contemplation there is “should” and “should not” (one should be apart from all marks in resolving, one should not dwell in form and give rise to mind, and so on), and in this gate of practice there is also “should” and “should not.” (This can be seen in the text and need not be quoted in full.) Earlier it said that where there is abiding there is wrongness, and here too it says one should not cling to empty or existent (the statements that marks are precisely non-marks and beings precisely non-beings are to make one comprehend this meaning in order to practice giving and so cling to neither extreme). Their sense echoes and answers each other at every point. Why is it so? If one has the wisdom of contemplation but does not practice it, it is empty talk; if one merely practices without the wisdom of contemplation, it is blind cultivation. Since the two gates assist each other and only then succeed, contemplation and practice must correspond. From this we can know that contemplation and practice must not only both be present, neither may be overemphasized. And from this we can further know that the principles spoken in the two gates of contemplation and practice must all be opened through, strung together, and fused. Contemplating thus, one practices thus; practicing thus, one contemplates thus. The least trace of biased dwelling is non-abiding. Why? Because it does not correspond. This is the essential point; you should know it thus.
(Chou) Second: Directly making clear the real. Two parts: (Yin) First, making clear that the teaching is real; second, making clear that the Dharma is real.
(Yin) First: Making clear that the teaching is real.
“Subhūti, the Tathāgata is one who speaks truly, speaks really, speaks as it is, speaks without deceit, speaks without difference.”

This section directly making clear the real shows that the meanings of non-abiding resolve and non-abiding giving spoken in the section just concluded are all known by personal realization, true and not false — to encourage faith.

“True” means that what is spoken is one and the same, that is, without difference. “Real” means that what is spoken is not empty, that is, without deceit. If these are matched with the dharmas, “true” means true thusness and “real” means true marks. This makes clear that all the words spoken above flowed forth one by one from true thusness and true marks; hence “one who speaks truly, one who speaks really.” Since every word accords with true thusness and true marks, He is one who speaks without deceit and without difference. That He says both “true speech” and “real speech” is not repetition; it carries a fine meaning.

You should know that the name “true thusness” expresses the emptiness and stillness of the substance of the nature, and is a name established solely with respect to the substance of the nature. For “true” means not delusive, making clear that it is not marks; “thus” means without difference, making clear that it is without self. Hence it was said above that if there are marks of self and person, one is not a bodhisattva; that whatever has marks is all delusive; that there is no mark of self, no mark of Dharma, and no mark of non-Dharma; that if the mind grasps at marks, whether it grasps at Dharma or non-Dharma, it clings to self, person, living being, and life; that one should be apart from all marks; and that one who is apart from marks is named a Buddha — all such words of emptying through to the bottom are what is meant by “one who speaks truly.” The intent is to cause people, relying on such words in cultivating contemplation and practice, to be apart from marks and forget the self, and thereby to realize and attest the true thusness that is markless, selfless, empty, still, and equal.

The name “true marks” expresses the nature’s virtue of being empty as-it-is and not empty as-it-is, and is a name established with respect to substance, mark, and function together. For “real” means neither real nor unreal, making clear that though marks are not the substance, they are the function of the substance, and function is not apart from substance. “Marks” means neither mark nor non-mark, making clear that though the substance is not marks, the substance must bring forth function, and function is not without marks. Hence it was said above that no living being is saved, and yet all living beings are saved; that one should dwell on nothing in regard to dharmas when practicing giving; that one should grasp neither Dharma nor non-Dharma; that it is “precisely not,” and again that it is “named thus”; that one should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing; and that one should give rise to a mind that dwells on nothing — all such words of both negating and illuminating, both dissolving and sustaining, the two extremes of empty and existent — are what is meant by “one who speaks really.” The intent is to cause people, relying on such words in cultivating contemplation and practice, to accord with perfect middle and to realize and attest the true marks that have substance and function, stillness and illumination simultaneous.

That He says both “without deceit” and “without difference” also carries its own deep meanings. For living beings have long been deluded about the true and chasing the delusive; hearing this true speech and real speech, they will surely be startled and terrified by it, taking it for the Milky Way and shrinking back in awe. So He earnestly and urgently tells them: “one who speaks without deceit” means that the Buddha does not deceive living beings. And fearing that the hearer may fail to understand deeply and wonder why He suddenly says “not” and suddenly says “is,” and why there are so many other self-contradicting statements; or that one who has first heard the incomplete teachings will further doubt why this sutra says something different again — He therefore adds the further earnest instruction: “one who speaks without difference” means that although various vehicles are spoken of, they are all the one Buddha-vehicle.

What is “speaking as it is”? It makes clear that all words are spoken as He personally realized them. Hence among the five kinds of speech, “as it is” is the main one. It lets one know that true speech and real speech are both personally realized to be so; they are by no means hearsay, so how could there be deceit? Words differ in a thousand ways, but principle returns to one; how could there be difference? Earnest encouragement to faith, with bitter words and a kind heart — this is the utmost. If not matched with the dharmas, it is like saying: all that I speak is both true and real. Because it is all spoken as I myself have realized it, every word is assuredly without deceit, and every word is not different from what I have realized. The reason “the Tathāgata” is named first is precisely to make clear that every word comes forth from the ocean of nature and every word accords with the virtue of nature. The five “who” are placed in sequence precisely to indicate that every word is certain and solid. All living beings need not be startled, need not be terrified, need not be afraid. Simply believe, understand, and uphold it thus, and speak it for others, and all will assuredly realize what I have personally realized. Hence the next section again speaks of the Dharma that is realized, to show that it is real and to encourage faith.
(Yin) Second: Making clear that the Dharma is real.
